**Interpretation.** $X = B(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$ is the Banach space of all *bounded functions* $x:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the supremum norm $\|x\|=\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}|x(t)|$. (If one insisted on reading $B(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ as bounded *linear* operators $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, every element has the form $x(t)=ct$; then $Tx(t)=c(t-\Delta)=ct-c\Delta$ is affine, not linear, so $T$ would not even map $X$ into $X$. Hence the bounded-functions reading is the only one under which the problem is well-posed.)

---

**Linearity.** Let $x,y\in X$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. For every $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
T(\alpha x+\beta y)(t)=(\alpha x+\beta y)(t-\Delta)=\alpha\,x(t-\Delta)+\beta\,y(t-\Delta)=\alpha\,(Tx)(t)+\beta\,(Ty)(t).
$$
Thus $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha\,Tx+\beta\,Ty$, so $T$ is linear.

**Boundedness and norm.** For any $x\in X$,
$$
\|Tx\|=\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}|(Tx)(t)|=\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}|x(t-\Delta)|.
$$
The map $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $\phi(t)=t-\Delta$, is a bijection, so $\{t-\Delta:t\in\mathbb{R}\}=\mathbb{R}$. Reindexing the supremum with $s=t-\Delta$,
$$
\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}|x(t-\Delta)|=\sup_{s\in\mathbb{R}}|x(s)|=\|x\|.
$$
Hence $\|Tx\|=\|x\|$ for every $x\in X$; $T$ is an isometry, therefore bounded, with
$$
\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le 1}\|Tx\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le 1}\|x\|=1.
$$
The bound is attained: the constant function $x\equiv 1$ satisfies $\|x\|=1$ and $\|Tx\|=1$.

**Conclusion.** $T$ is linear and bounded, and $\|T\|=1$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
